title: The talents (Matthew 25:14–30)
hookLine: two servants risk what they were given; the third buries his out of fear

cards: A rich man is leaving on a long journey. He calls in three servants and hands over his fortune: five talents to one, two to the next, one to the third. Each, the story says, according to his ability.
The first two go straight out, trade, and double what they were given. The third walks to a quiet spot, digs a hole, and buries his. Safe.
Nobody can steal it. A long time later the master comes home to settle accounts. Two servants walk in with double.
The third walks in with dirt still on the coins.

teach.h: A TALENT WAS A WEIGHT OF SILVER.
teach.b: Here's the surprise: a talent wasn't a skill. It was a large weight of silver, a fortune in coin. Even the one-talent servant was handed a fortune.

The usual account is that our English word talent, meaning a gift or ability, grew out of this very story: Christians took the talents to mean the gifts God gives each person, and over time the word changed meaning.
A story, so the account goes, rewrote a dictionary. The master says the same words to the first two, in the old King James Bible: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant."

teach.h: I WAS AFRAID, AND HID IT.
teach.b: Then the third speaks, and he's honest about why: "I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth." He didn't waste it. He didn't steal it.
He just couldn't bear the risk. And the ending is hard: his talent is taken and given away, and he's thrown out. Christians read this in more than one way.
Some hear it about gifts: whatever you've been given, however small, is meant to be used, not hidden.
Some read it about waiting: it sits among Jesus's stories of the end of the age, a call to stay faithful until he comes back.

teach.h: GIFTS, WAITING, OR A HARD MASTER?
teach.b: Some notice that the third servant calls the master a hard man, reaping where he never sowed, and ask whether this master is meant to be God at all.

teach.h: WELL DONE, THOU GOOD AND FAITHFUL SERVANT.
teach.b: Churches hold these readings side by side. On one thing the story is clear: it won't praise burying what you were given.

how: Christians often read the parable of the talents as a call to use the gifts God has given them in service of others, and churches often preach on it when inviting people to volunteer or give.

o: a natural gift or skill for something
a loan paid back with interest
a large weight of silver, a fortune

p: why the third servant hid it

s: in the story, a talent means a skill
a talent was a large weight of silver, a fortune. the usual account is that the skill meaning grew out of this parable.
the third servant lost the money
he gave back every coin. he buried it because he was afraid.
the first two servants hear the same words
"well done, thou good and faithful servant" to each.

games.q: you're the third servant. you've been handed one talent, a fortune, and your master is gone for a long time. what do you do?
o: trade with it and try to double it.
dig a hole and bury it where it's safe.
spend it and hope he never comes back.
games.why: he buries it: "I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth." the story's hard ending falls on the one who played it safe.

practice: Bring to mind something you're good at, or used to be, that you've put in the ground: singing, fixing things, listening, writing, making people laugh. Ask, gently, what you were afraid of: being bad at it, or being seen.
If you pray, offer it back to God; if not, just hold it in your hands again for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Talent. A large weight of silver, entrusted to a servant. By the usual account, this story is why the English word came to mean a gift.

orig.note: Greek: a balance, and then a weight — a large sum of silver money.

carryVoice: Your line: fear buries things. Even the smallest gift wasn't meant for the ground. Week five, under way.
